title: Show HN: What [67] MCP servers do at startup, with the internet cut off
content:
Level 1 measurements
7 of 67 servers reached for a website their own README does not name
Each of those 7 servers is recorded with the name it asked for and the line of its README that does not contain it. Nothing left the machine: the room has no route off the host, so every name answered to the loopback address and no connection completed.
24 servers offered a tool their README does not name — 1,143 tools were offered in total and none was called. Read that second figure with the caveat attached: this rule reads only the README that shipped in the package, so a server documenting its tools in a reference file beside it shows every tool as unnamed, and 10 of those servers have a README under three kilobytes. A large count here is a fact about the rule as much as about the package.
2 did both. The remaining 38 had nothing found, which is not the same as a clean sweep — see below.
67 npm packages, each measured from its name alone: installed, started in a room with no route to the internet and no real credentials, asked for its list of tools, and compared against its own README. No tool was called. Measured 2026-10-31.
Not calibration-backed. The calibration behind the ten curated measurements proves the instrument catches planted claims about what a tool did. Level 1 calls no tool and reads each README by a stated rule rather than by a person, so nothing in that calibration speaks to these pages.
A website counts as declared only if the README names it. A tool counts as documented only if the README names it as a whole word.
This is not a ranking of the most-used servers. The set measured is whatever two registry searches returned, read by hand for whether each package is a server that starts without a credential. Download figures decided nothing about the order of this table, which is alphabetical by package, and four widely used servers are measured here that neither search returned at all. Nothing on this page says one server is more used, better or worse than another.
Reading the table
- Published at is the repository or homepage the package's own manifest points at, printed because two packages measured here are called Playwright and are not by the same people. It is what each package says about itself and is not verified.
- Tools offered is what each server answered to one tools/list request. None was called.
- Websites reached for counts the distinct names a server looked up or opened an encrypted connection to before any tool was used. Nothing left the machine: every name answered to the loopback address, so no connection completed and no contents were seen.
- Not named in the README is the comparison, by the rule above and nothing looser. "none" means every tool it offered and every website it reached for appears in its own README.
- An empty row is not a clean sweep. A server that offers few tools and reaches for no website has little for this comparison to find, which is a fact about the measurement as much as about the server.
- A large count is not a scandal either. Only the README file that shipped in the package is read. A server that documents its tools in another file — a reference page beside the README, or a website — shows every tool it offers as not named here. Each report cites the README it read, its digest and its line count, and the name it looked for and did not find, so any row can be checked rather than taken.
- It is one run, once, with no route off the machine and no tool called. A page here says what a server did at startup while being watched, and where its README was silent about it. It says nothing else.
All 67 packages started, so no row says could not start. Evidence for every row — the full trace, the tool list, the README digest and each citation — is in level1/evidence/, one JSON file per package, beside the code that produced it.
29 pages are not published yet. Each reports a finding, and a page reporting a finding goes up only after its maintainers have been notified and three days have passed. The counts above include them; the pages and the package names do not appear until then. [How that works](/method.html)

report.summary: A researcher started 67 npm MCP servers with no internet access and found 7 contacted undeclared websites and 24 exposed tools their own READMEs never mention.
report.background: Anthropic introduced the Model Context Protocol in late 2024 as a standard way for AI assistants to call external tools and data sources, and the ecosystem has since exploded into hundreds of community npm packages. Because an MCP server typically runs as a local process with the user's own privileges, it can read files, hold API keys and open outbound connections — yet almost nobody audits what these packages do before a single tool is invoked. Well-publicised MCP issues around tool poisoning, prompt injection and unvetted third-party servers have made supply-chain visibility a live concern. This project applies a minimal, reproducible instrument: install each package, start it in a network-isolated room, ask for its tool list once, and diff the observed behaviour against the documentation that shipped with it.
key_points: Seven of the 67 servers looked up or opened an encrypted connection to a website their own README never names — and this happened at startup, before any tool was called. Nothing actually left the machine because the test room had no route off the host, but the intent to phone home was recorded by name.

Twenty-four servers advertised at least one tool their README does not mention; 1,143 tools were offered in total across the set and none of them was invoked. Two packages both reached for undeclared sites and offered undocumented tools; the other 38 showed nothing the rule could catch.

The method is deliberately narrow and the author says so repeatedly: only the README shipped inside the package is read, so a server that documents tools in a side file or on a website will look fully undocumented. Large counts are as much a fact about the rule as about the package.

It is one run, once, with no credentials and no tool calls, and the author explicitly states it is not a ranking — download figures decided nothing, ordering is alphabetical, and an empty row means 'little to find', not 'clean'.
Every row ships with its full trace, tool list, README digest and the exact missing name in level1/evidence/, and 29 findings are withheld until maintainers are notified and three days pass.
report.impact: For the AI industry this is a small but pointed demonstration that MCP's supply chain is currently unobservable: you cannot tell from a package page what a server does the moment it starts. Expect pressure toward declared network egress, signed manifests, and tool inventories that can be diffed automatically — the kind of hygiene npm itself never fully achieved. For developers building MCP servers, the lesson is blunt: document every tool you expose and every host you contact, because someone will eventually compare your README to your behaviour in public. For regular users the practical takeaway is that installing an MCP server is closer to running an unvetted binary than installing a plugin, and it inherits whatever access your assistant already has.
report.tools: To follow up, try the official MCP Inspector for listing a server's tools before you trust it, and Invariant Labs' mcp-scan for static and runtime checks on MCP configurations. Docker's --network none or a firejail/netns sandbox reproduces this experiment cheaply, and mitmproxy or a DNS sinkhole logs which hosts a process reaches for. npm pack --dry-run plus the published tarball shows exactly which docs shipped, and Semgrep rules can flag outbound calls at server init.
